passage:
Subject: Smart boards and results, before we send the funders' report

Hi Ira,
I know the draft says the smart boards "raised Class 8 scores by 14 marks". The link is real in the data. I'm just not ready to say the boards caused it, and I'd like one more week.
Three things are bothering me. First, the twelve schools that got boards are mostly in the ward with more teachers per class. That alone could explain better scores. Second, the direction: the district gave boards first to schools that were already doing well, as a reward. Third, it's one year of results, and one year can swing by chance.
What I'd like to do is compare them with the eight schools on the waiting list that look most like them, same ward, same teacher numbers, same scores two years ago. If the gap holds there, I'll sign the sentence happily.
Aadhya

qa.q: How many schools on the waiting list does Aadhya want to compare with?
qa.a: The eight schools on the waiting list that look most like the board schools.

qa.q: What is Aadhya worried about if the report goes out as drafted?
qa.a: Aadhya is worried the report will claim the boards caused the higher scores when more teachers, the district rewarding strong schools, or a lucky year could explain the link.

qa.q: Which step in Aadhya's plan is the strongest, and why?
qa.a: Comparing with the most similar waiting-list schools, because it shows what scores looked like without boards, so any gap left is more likely due to the boards.

qa.q: How might Ira feel reading this email just before the funders' report?
qa.a: Ira may feel a bit frustrated by the delay but also relieved that a claim the funders might check has been tested before it goes out.

grounding: It shows a careful analyst asking whether a third cause, reverse direction or chance explains a link, and seeking a comparison group before claiming cause.

Jyoti, you asked on the show what I actually do at the academy. Okay, here's one story.
Last season the head coach showed me a chart. Players who did the new video sessions improved their batting average far more than players who didn't. He wanted to make them compulsory and buy three more cameras.
I'm the analyst, so my first question was, who chose which players went to the video sessions? Turns out the coaches picked the ones they thought were "about to break through". So the players were already rising. That's the direction problem.
Then I asked what else those players had. Extra net time, as it happened. Third cause.
So we ran it properly. Next term, among players the coaches rated the same, half got video sessions by draw and half didn't. The video group did improve, a little. Much less than the chart. We bought one camera, not three.
Ankita, analyst. That's the job.

qa.q: How many cameras did the academy finally buy?
qa.a: One camera, not three.

qa.q: What did Ankita think might be wrong with the head coach's chart at first?
qa.a: Ankita suspected the chart looked better than the truth, because coaches had picked players who were already rising and those players also had extra net time.

qa.q: Which choice made Ankita's approach convincing, and why?
qa.a: Splitting similarly rated players by draw into video and no-video groups; it removed the coaches' choices and the extra net time as explanations, so the small real effect could be seen.

qa.q: How might the head coach have felt when the proper test showed a much smaller gain?
qa.a: The head coach might have been disappointed after hoping for a big win, but also better placed to spend money on what actually helps players.

grounding: It shows a careful analyst checking reverse direction and a third cause, then using a fair comparison group before claiming the video sessions helped.

Last Wednesday each child planted two bean seeds in a cup. On Thursday, Ujjwal, 8, whistled a tune to his cup before lunch. On Saturday both his seeds sprouted.
Today he told the class, "I whistled to them and they came out. Whistling makes beans grow." Two children started whistling at their cups at once.
Kishore pointed out that his own beans had sprouted too, and he had never whistled. Ujjwal said, "Maybe you hummed and forgot."
I didn't tell him he was wrong. I asked the class to set up two new cups each: whistle to one, keep the other quiet, and draw both every morning.
Next: check the drawings on Friday and let Ujjwal say what he sees first.

qa.a: On Saturday both his seeds sprouted.

qa.a: Setting up two cups each, one with whistling and one without, lets Ujjwal see for himself whether the whistling changes anything, instead of being told he is wrong.

qa.a: Ujjwal might feel embarrassed and stop sharing ideas, and he would miss the chance to test it himself with the two cups.

Madhav, fifteen, held his report card up in the auto on the way home from school in Nagpur. Second term: 81 percent. First term: 64.
"It's the focus app," he told Shankar. "I started it in October. Twenty-five minutes study, five minutes break, and the little tree grows. That's it. That's the whole secret."
Shankar looked out at the traffic. "October is also when you stopped going to your cousin's wedding every weekend. And when your family finished shifting house."
"Yeah, but the app is what changed my brain."
"First term you were new in the school too."
"Everyone's new sometime." Madhav was already showing the auto driver the little tree on his phone. "I'm telling my whole tuition batch to download it."
Shankar shrugged and let it go.

qa.a: First term: 64.

qa.q: Why does Madhav feel so certain the app raised his marks?
qa.a: He started the app in October and the marks went up after, so the timing feels like proof, and he brushes aside the wedding weekends, the house shift and being new.

qa.q: What could Madhav check before telling his whole tuition batch?
qa.a: He could ask whether his marks would have risen anyway once the move, the weddings and being new were over, and see if others who use the app improve too.

qa.a: Shankar thinks the settled home and free weekends explain the jump, and seems tired of arguing when Madhav won't listen.

grounding: It shows a teenager crediting an app for scoring well when his results may simply have improved as his life settled down.

Usha kept reading them and then putting the phone face down. She said, "Everyone's so sure. What if I don't try it and it gets worse?" She looked tired and a bit cornered.

qa.a: It adds pressure and guilt when Usha just wants to rest, because each confident message makes her feel she is doing something wrong by not trying it.

In Khejarli village the monsoon had just ended, and Nazia was sure. "My ammi's knee pain stopped the week she started the copper bangle. It works, Shreya."
Shreya, twenty-four, who taught at the village school, sat with her on the step. "I'm happy it stopped. But her knee always gets worse in the damp months, na? Would it have eased anyway once the rains ended?"

Last spring I was put in charge of the new night-shift break room at our call centre in Mohali. I'm Revathi, the first woman shift lead there, and I was sure I knew what people wanted: a quiet room, soft lights, a shelf of books, herbal tea. That's what I'd want.

qa.a: All sixty people on nights.

qa.a: Checking what people actually wanted with the form and by sitting with colleagues unlike her, instead of ordering what she herself would enjoy.

qa.a: Naveen and Suraj probably feel noticed and welcome, since they were asked, and the room now has the carrom board and microwave people like them wanted.

Keerthana from next door, watching from the doorway, said, "Faisal, she doesn't even know how to hold her fingers yet."
Faisal opened his mouth to argue, then looked at Ayesha's hand, flat on the board with her thumb sticking out, and went quiet.

qa.q: Where did the striker go when Ayesha first flicked it?
qa.a: It spun off the board and under the sofa.

qa.q: Why does Faisal get so frustrated with Ayesha?
qa.a: The shot is so easy for Faisal that he can't remember not knowing it, so he thinks she isn't listening when she is actually missing the first steps.

qa.q: What turning point came for Faisal, and what could he do next?
qa.a: Looking at Ayesha's flat hand after Keerthana spoke; he could start by showing her how to hold her fingers before any cut shots.

qa.q: How might Keerthana see the lesson from the doorway?
qa.a: Keerthana can see what Faisal can't: Ayesha is missing the very first step, and the shouting is only making her more lost.

grounding: It shows an older boy teaching his little sister carrom, skipping steps that seem obvious to him, and getting frustrated when she is lost.

"But you said six means six!"
"Amma! She's not trying!"
Shalini came in drying her hands. "Karthik, when did you learn clocks?"
"I don't know. Always?"
"You learned in Class 2, and you cried for a week. Tell her what the big hand does first. Just the big hand."
Karthik sighed, then pointed. "Okay. This one is the minute hand. It goes all the way round in one hour."

qa.q: What time did Karthik show first?
qa.a: Four o'clock, with the big hand on twelve and the small hand on four.

qa.q: Why does Karthik think Kavitha is not trying?
qa.a: Reading a clock feels like something he has always known, so he skips why the six can mean half past and blames her when she gets lost.

qa.q: What choice by Amma turned the lesson around?
qa.a: Reminding Karthik that he once struggled too, and telling him to start with only the big hand, so he begins from the step Kavitha is missing.

qa.q: What is it like for Kavitha when Karthik says six means half past?
qa.a: It is confusing and a little upsetting, because he first said the number meant the hour, and now the same number means something else and she is being scolded for it.

grounding: It shows an older boy teaching his little sister the clock, skipping steps that seem obvious to him and getting frustrated when she is lost.
